newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French cenbanker against a too strong euro.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French cenbanker against a too strong euro.

text.p: Europe must avoid launching a single currency which is too strong against the dollar if it is to tackle its problems of mass unemployment, a member of the Bank of France's monetary policy council said on Tuesday.

Paul Marchelli, one of nine members of the council, also said France should cut interest rates as soon as possible, even taking these below German interest rates, to revive growth. This could be done without destabilising the franc.
"Europe will only be made by the people...people today are asking questions, because they fear a Europe of the unemployed," he told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"They will not accept us building Europe any old way," he said in an unusually public warning from a member of the central bank's highly secretive inner sanctum.
Europe must push for a better exchange rate against a dollar which was undervalued against most European currencies. Setting the euro at parity with the dollar "would be a good thing".

His comments came a week after former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing broke a taboo on questioning France's decade-old commitment to a strong franc by arguing for a franc depreciation before monetary union in 1999.

Giscard d'Estaing, who revived the entire debate over the merits of monetary union, repeated his call for a weaker franc in a radio interview on Tuesday, and rounded on critics who attacked him for airing the issue.
Bank of France council member Jean Boissonnat on Sunday likened Giscard d'Estaing's call to the behaviour of a child who breaks a toy to draw attention to himself.

"This is a problem which concerns all French people because it's linked to the economy's health and to unemployment," said Giscard d'Estaing. The debate should not the "clandestine" reserve of central bankers, he said.
Marchelli argued that the debate on the strong franc was really about exchange rate policy after monetary union.
"We are seeing the start of the big debate on what the dollar-euro parity will be," Marchelli said.
The euro would be a strong currency in the future, but "it would be a mistake to try to have a euro which is as strong as possible at the start," as this would damage Europe's economies.
The question threatens to create tensions with Germany, whose leaders want to reassure a doubting public that the euro will be as strong as the mark it replaces.

Many economists expect the future European Central Bank (ECB), to be based in Frankfurt, to behave similarly to the Bundesbank and be just as hawkish in its readiness to push up interest rates to defend the euro's stability.

Marchelli said no one country should be allowed to dominate the ECB. But it would be wrong to think that Germany was making all the decisions on monetary union, or that it even wanted to be seen as dictating these matters.
Marchelli, former head of the white-collar CGC trade union, was also quoted by daily Liberation earlier as saying that the policy of linking the franc to the mark was "sterile".
Marchelli told Reuters he felt France could afford to cut interest rates without waiting for Germany to move first but he was not arguing for a devaluation of the franc against the mark.
"We could quite easily give ourselves a bit of autonomy in interest rate matters," he said.
The franc was solid and a rate cut should not hurt. "The sooner the better seems the best solution to me. All conditions are in place for us to make this cut," he said.
He declined to say by how much he thought the Bank could cut its intervention rate, now at 3.20 percent, just a fifth of a percent higher than Germany's key repo interest rate.
The Bank of France has traditionally maintained a small premium in French rates over German rates to cushion the franc against any speculative attack on currency markets.
According to Liberation, Marchelli is one of three members of the monetary policy council arguing for faster rate cuts.
But two of the remaining six -- journalist Jean Boissonat and banker Bruno de Maulde -- see their terms of office expire at the end of the year.
This will provide President Jacques Chirac, who wants to see rates come down to help the economy, with a chance to tip the balance within the Bank if he wants to.
The replacements will be chosen by the government on the recommendations of the presidents of the upper and lower houses of parliament and the Economic and Social Council.
